lines.text: In seventeen forty-one, on a beach in southern India,
a Dutch commander surrendered to an Indian king.
Then he did something stranger:
he joined that king's army,
and served it for the rest of his life.
To see how he got there, we go back to Amsterdam,
and a very new idea:
a company that could go to war.
In fifteen ninety-six,
Cornelis de Howtman's ships reached Java,
and the Dutch had their own route to the spices.
Back home, they were fighting Spain for independence,
and Spain now ruled Portugal too,
so hurting the Portuguese in Asia
was business and revenge at once.
In sixteen-oh-two, the Dutch government
merged its rival trading firms into one:
the Dutch East India Company.
Ordinary citizens could buy shares.
And it could do what few companies ever had:
build forts, sign treaties,
mint coins, and wage war.
Their first factory, on the Koro-man-del coast,
opened at Mussoo-lee-putnam in sixteen-oh-five.
Soon came Poo-lee-kat, north of Madras,
where they built a fort and minted copper coins.
Poo-lee-kat alone may have had
over a thousand handlooms working for them.
But why India, if the Dutch wanted spices?
Because the Spice Islands wanted Indian cloth.
So they ran a loop: buy cotton cloth in India,
trade it for nutmeg, cloves and pepper in Indonesia,
and sell those in Europe.
Along the way they carried indigo, silk from Bengal,
saltpetre from Bihar for gunpowder,
and opium and rice from the Ganga valley.
The English wanted the same spices,
and the rivalry turned ugly.
In sixteen twenty-three, on the island of Am-boy-na,
the Dutch accused English traders
of plotting to seize their fort.
After confessions taken under torture,
they executed ten Englishmen,
nine Japanese soldiers
and one Portuguese man.
It ended any hope of the two companies working together.
The Dutch kept the Spice Islands,
and the English turned more and more to India.
Meanwhile, they went after their old enemy.
As R. C. Mozoom-dar and his co-authors put it,
the Dutch had two aims in the East:
revenge on Spain and Portugal,
and a monopoly of the spice trade.
In sixteen fifty-eight
they took Naaga-putti-num from the Portuguese,
far down the Koro-man-del coast.
In sixteen sixty-three they took Cochin,
and with it, Portugal's last Mala-bar forts.
For a while, Kerala's pepper ran through Dutch hands.
Not everything they did was about money.
Cochin's Dutch governor, Hendrik van Ray-duh,
set out to record the useful plants of Kerala.
His key expert was Itty Ah-choo-dun,
a local Eezha-va physician,
checked by three Kon-kunee Brahmin scholars.
The result, the Hortus Mala-barry-kus,
came out in twelve volumes from sixteen seventy-eight,
with almost eight hundred engravings.
It is one of the earliest great books on tropical plants,
built on Indian knowledge.
Now, back to that beach.
By the seventeen-thirties,
King Maar-taanda Varma of Travan-kor
was taking over the pepper coast,
and the Dutch sent troops to stop him.
In August seventeen forty-one, at Ko-la-chel,
the story goes that a Travan-kor cannonball
set off a Dutch gunpowder barrel,
their rice supply went up with it,
and soon the Dutch surrendered.
Local fishermen are said to have helped too,
sinking Dutch boats at night.
Their commander, Yoo-stah-kee-us De Lan-wah,
was taken prisoner, and then recruited.
He trained Travan-kor's army in European drill
and rose to command it.
Twelve years later, the Dutch signed a treaty
promising not to stand in Travan-kor's way.
In Bengal, the Dutch made one last move.
After Plassey, Nawab Meer Jaa-far
secretly invited them in to balance the British,
and in seventeen fifty-nine
a Dutch fleet sailed up the Hoog-lee
carrying more than fifteen hundred soldiers.
The British, under Colonel Francis Forde, struck first,
on the river and then on land near Chin-soo-ra.
Only sixteen Europeans got through to the fort.
Then the British replaced Meer Jaa-far
with his son-in-law, Meer Kaa-sim,
and tightened their grip on Bengal.
After that, the Dutch faded.
Their real profits were in Indonesia,
and in seventeen ninety-five British forces
took most of their posts in India.
The company was wound up in seventeen ninety-nine.
By a treaty with Britain in eighteen twenty-four,
they gave up the rest, handing it over in eighteen twenty-five.
They came to India for trade, not empire,
and they left the same way.
The one Dutch commander who stayed behind
did it as a soldier of an Indian king.
